newsitem.title: USA: World gold demand down 4 pct so far in 1996 - WGC.
newsitem.headline: World gold demand down 4 pct so far in 1996 - WGC.

text.p: World gold demand in the 10 largest gold consuming markets slipped to 1,566 tonnes in the first nine months of 1996, four percent below the record levels in the same period last year, World Gold Council (WGC) said Wednesday.

"The most significant fall came in Japan where investment demand fell to 51.1 tonnes in the first nine months, down 61 percent from 133.1 tonnes in the same period last year," WGC North American economist Richard Scott-Ram said in a presentation of the Council's third-quarter demand estimates.
Investment demand in third-quarter 1996 in Japan was down 53 pct at 15.0 tonnes from third-quarter 1995.
"The weaker yen more than offset the decline in the U.S. dollar gold price resulting in profit taking from those who bought gold a year ago at around 1,100 yen," Scott-Ram said.
The dollar reached a 42-month high against yen earlier this month.
"Continued soft jewelry demand coupled with sharply lower investment interest brought (Japanese) consumption in the third quarter to the lowest levels in recent times at 44 tonnes," he said.
U.S. gold demand remained strong, setting a third-quarter record of 89.8 tonnes, reflecting buoyant jewelry demand, steady dental consumption and a stabilization of coin demand.
U.S. jewelry demand rose four percent to 85 tonnes in the third quarter from the same period last year, with the expansion of U.S. gold jewelry sales now in its fifth year.
Year-to-date U.S. jewellry demand was up 7 percent.
Aggregate third-quarter developed country demand of 200.7 tonnes was seven percent below third-quarter 1995, mostly as a result of a 44 pct fall in investment demand.
Among developing countries, India, the world's largest gold consuming country, saw demand down four percent at 114.1 tonnes in the third quarter of this year.

"This weaker tone in demand is attributed to a slowdown in industrial output coinciding with an inauspicious buying period in the Hindi calendar associated with a leap month," Scott-Ram said. "The effect of the leap month is that this year trade purchases in anticipation of the 'Diwali' festival season fall entirely within the fourth quarter, whereas last year the third quarter benefitted from festival demand."
But year-to-date Indian demand of 365 tonnes is still running one percent above the same period last year.
Overall, developing country gold demand set a record 453.8 tonnes in third-quarter 1996, just ahead of the 453.3 tonnes in the same quarter last year.
Total world gold demand slipped two percent in the third quarter to 654.8 tonnes, WGC detailed.
Spot gold had an average price of $384.61 an ounce in the third quarter, $5.44 below second-quarter 1996 but a fraction higher than third-quarter 1995, according to the Council.

"But it is worth pointing out the fourth quarter is customarily a time of comparative tightness as the flexibility of some central bank lenders is constrained by domestic book-keeping needs," Scott-Ram said.

Last year, this coincided with a period of substantial producer hedging associated with project financing and the market went briefly into an unusual backwardation in November as short-term lease rates soared above long term rates.
Gold lease rates rose steadily in the third quarter this year too, WGC said.
One month gold lease rates rose to 2.22 pct in October while 12 month rates rose to 2.52 pct in late September.
Meanwhile, official sector gold holdings, as published by the IMF, showed a net fall of 970,000 ounces (30.2 tonnes) between June and July 1996.
The largest falls occurred in South Africa (down 19.6 tonnes) and in Poland (down 13.1 tonnes).
Total official sector holdings were estimated at 1106.1 million ounces (34,403 tonnes) at the end of the third quarter 1996, down from 1113.3 million ounces at the end of 1995.
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities, +1-212-859-1641.
